bib.title: Computer Age Statistical Inference, Chapter 6: Empirical Bayes

question: How can a large collection of parallel cases supply the prior information Bayes' rule needs, so each case can be estimated from the others?
contributions: Robbins' formula: E{theta|x} = (x+1) f(x+1)/f(x), estimated from counts with no prior
Missing-species (Fisher / Good-Toulmin) estimator for unseen categories
Parametric (gamma) and log-polynomial-prior empirical Bayes fits

results.claim: In the nodes study, 340 of 844 patients (40%) had observed ratio p=x/n equal to zero.
results.setup: 844 cancer surgeries; n=nodes removed (1 to 69, mean 19, sd 11), x=positive nodes

results.claim: Empirical Bayes prior (4th-degree log-polynomial, MLE) shrinks the zero spike: Pr{theta<=0.01}=0.12 vs 38% of raw p below 0.01.
results.setup: Nodes study N=844, binomial x_k~Bi(n_k,theta_k), log g = polynomial deg 4 in theta

results.claim: Estimated prior puts 0.59 of its mass below theta=0.2 and 0.07 above 0.8.
For the patient with 3 positives of 6 nodes the raw estimate is 0.50 and the empirical Bayes posterior mean is 0.446 (shrinkage toward the bulk).

limits: Robbins' empirical formula is unstable where counts are small (right end of Table 6.1).
Good-Toulmin estimate (6.19) is unstable for t>1; the gamma prior extrapolation is 'a mathematical convenience, not a fact of nature' and far-future projections are 'educated guessing'.
Standard errors (+-178, +-11.2, bars in Figs 6.2 and 6.4) assume independence among species/cases; the point estimates do not.
The nodes prior assumes a 4th-degree polynomial log-density; error bars hold only if that model is adequate. Computation deferred to Chapter 21.
Chapter does not discuss winner's curse or James-Stein shrinkage explicitly; that is Chapter 7. Only the 3/6 -> 0.446 example shows shrinkage.
Shakespeare 'Shall I die?' test: predicted 6.97 vs 9 observed, inconclusive.
practices: Use Robbins' formula (6.7) when the prior is unknown but many parallel cases exist (p.77).
Prefer a parametric prior fit when empirical counts are small, as it gives less noisy estimates (p.77).
Treat extrapolation beyond t=1 in missing-species problems as educated guessing (p.81).
Check that independence assumptions behind standard errors hold (p.89).

terms.definition: Bayesian formula (6.5) for a single subject is estimated empirically (i.e., frequentistically) from a collection of similar cases.
E{theta|x} = (x+1) f(x+1)/f(x), eq 6.5; empirical version (x+1) y_{x+1}/y_x, eq 6.7
proportion of the total sum of theta_k corresponding to the species unseen in the original trapping period; estimated by y1/N
Direct evidence: each subject's outcome bears directly on the question; indirect: relevance of other cases in a large data set to the case of interest.
